UN ENTITIES OPERATING IN NORTH
MACEDONIA
7As an upper-middle income country and
European Union (EU) accession state with a
vibrant and diverse population, the Republic
of North Macedonia (henceforth ‘North
Macedonia’) is well positioned to build on its
previous achievements, overcome remaining
challenges, and accelerate its progress towards
inclusive and sustainable development.
The Government of North Macedonia has
demonstrated and maintained a steadfast
commitment to the 2030 Agenda and the
Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), and
the overarching principle of leaving no one
behind.
The development and launch of the National
Development Strategy 2024–2044 (NDS)
represented a significant milestone in
articulating a detailed roadmap and national
priorities for the country for the coming two
decades, providing an overarching framework
against which national and international
development partners can align their support.
The development of this new UN Cooperation
Framework 2026–2030 was informed by a
comprehensive, integrated, and multisectoral
analysis of the situation and needs in the
country, as well as an independent evaluation
of the previous UN Cooperation Framework
2021–2025. Extensive consultations with
Government counterparts, international
development partners, civil society, and other
stakeholders were also undertaken to ensure
inclusiveness and inform interventions so that
they meet the needs of all people in North
Macedonia, particularly those at risk of being
left behind.
As the UN Cooperation Framework represents
the UN’s collective offer in support of the
Government of North Macedonia’s national
development priorities, identification of the
below interconnected and mutually reinforcing
Strategic Priorities was also heavily informed by
and aligned to the NDS.
• Strategic Priority 1: Inclusive Social and
Human Development
• Strategic Priority 2: Sustainable Economy
and Decent Work
• Strategic Priority 3: Resilient and Green
Society and Ecosystems
• Strategic Priority 4: Rule of Law and Good
Governance
These Strategic Priorities and associated
outcome also contribute to the EU’s‘Western
Balkans Reform and Growth Facility 2024–
2027’ that outline the milestones to be met
towards North Macedonia’s accession to the
bloc. The UN Cooperation Framework also
reflects the‘Six Transitions’where appropriate
as catalysts to accelerate progress towards the
SDGs. In addition, through the configuration
process, the United Nations has identified the
necessary expertise, as well as the technical
and financial capacities, to provide the required
support for achieving the agreed targets.
Strategic oversight and coordination of UN
Cooperation Framework implementation will
be undertaken through a UN-Government
Joint Steering Committee. Technical level
operationalization and coordination of the
Framework will be undertaken through
dedicated Results Groups, one per priority,
comprised of relevant UN system entities,
Government partners, and other stakeholders
as appropriate.Transparency and accountability
for delivery of results will be ensured through
formulation of joint workplans, annual review
processes, and publication of annual results
reports.
As a statement of intent to supporting North
Macedonia’s national development priorities
overthe coming years, the UN, through this UN
CooperationFramework,willremain committed
to the continued advancement of the SDGs in
this final phase of the 2030 Agenda.
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
8A landlock country in the Western Balkans with
1.8 million citizens, North Macedonia has made
considerable gains on its path towards the 2030
Agenda and has demonstrated its commitment
to sustainable development and aligning its
ambitions to the SDGs.
TheGovernment prepared aVoluntaryNational
Review (VNR) in 2020 as a baseline of where
the country stood vis-à-vis the SDGs. The VNR
found significant progress under the‘People’
and ‘Prosperity’categories, including on
poverty, unemployment, inequality. However,
critical challenges persist in the areas of Quality
Education (SDG 4), Gender Equality (SDG 5),
Decent Work and Economic Growth (SDG
8), and Reduced Inequalities (SDG 10). While
efforts have increased in recent years, a number
of challenges were identified under the‘Planet’
category, particularly related to the country’s
reliance offossilfuels and high levels of pollution
which hinder progress on Affordable and Clean
Energy (SDG 7) and Sustainable Cities and
Communities (SDG 11). Various challenges also
persist related to Peace, Justice, and Strong
Institutions (SDG 16)thatlimit progress against
all other SDG areas.
The UN Country Analysis undertaken to inform
the development of the UN Cooperation
Framework identified nine strategic challenges
that hinder SDG progress: 1) Low economic
competitiveness; 2) Declining quality of life; 3)
Insufficient social inclusion; 5) Limited energy
security; 5) High environmental pollution; 6)
Low institutionalresilience; 7) Weak rule of law,
including prevalent corruption; 8) Insufficient
public services; and 9) Weak public finance
management.
Country Context
Since the start of the EU accession process in
2001, North Macedonia has remained fully
committed to the Euro-Atlantic integration,
including EU accession, with most citizens
having a positive view on EU integration.
The country’s strategic location at the
crossroads of key European trade corridors
and access to EU markets — with over 78 per
cent of exports are directed to the EU — offers
significant potential for economic growth and
integrationintoglobalvaluechains. Despitethis,
economic competitiveness remains weak and
economic growth is sluggish averaging around
two per cent over the past decade — the lowest
compared to other Western Balkan countries.
Although having decreased from 36 per cent to
24per centofGDPbetween2006and2021,the
informal economy remains large, undermining
fair competition and limiting national revenues.
The country’s export base is narrow, with heavy
reliance on automotive, textile, and metal
industries, while high-tech exports constituted
only 5.2 per cent of manufactured exports
in 2023. Consequently, boosting economic
competitiveness and diversification will require
strategic investments and reforms in high-value
industries and green and digital sectors, with an
emphasis on strengthening small and medium
enterprises.
Significant progress has been made in reducing
unemployment since 2010, although rates
remain high, standing at 13.2 per cent in 2023
(female 11.4 per cent; male 14.4 per cent),
with youth unemployment reaching 29.7 per
cent. Roma unemployment is 67 per cent,
with only 8 per cent of Roma women formally
employed. Persons with disabilities also face
high unemployment rates and barriers to public
services. Economic empowerment of women
— including through family-friendly policies,
particularly expansion of early childhood
education and care — would help address low
female labour force participation (standing at
41.3 per cent compared to 61.5 per cent for
men) and labour shortages. (SDG 8)
While the country claims an upper-middle
income status with a high level of human
PROGRESS TOWARDS THE 2030 AGENDA
9development according the 2022 Human
Development Index (0.765 up from 0.762 in
2015), high poverty rates remain persistent,
standing at 23 per cent in 2022, with rates
reaching 32.2 per cent among children, and up
to 79 per cent for Roma children. , Poverty is
also higher in rural areas, standing at nearly
30 per cent compared to 17 per cent in urban
areas. (SDG 1)
However, the average life expectancy is 70.9
years for men and 75.2 years for women (3.3
years below the European average), while there
is an almost 9-year gap between life expectancy
andhealthylifeexpectancy. (SDG3)Thecountry
alsohasdeclining learningoutcomes—including
due to COVID-19 related disruptions — with
significant gaps compared to EU levels. Up to 74
per cent of 15-year-olds lack basic proficiency in
reading and mathematics, while Roma and lowincome children disproportionately fall below
national averages. (SDG 4)
North Macedonia’s energy system is marked by
high import dependency (around 30 per cent
of consumed energy), high energy intensity
(nearly three times the EU average), and strong
reliance on coal (47 per cent of electricity
generation). Energy poverty remains significant,
with almost 23.8 per cent unable to heat their
homes in winter. While accounting forjust 19.5
per cent of total energy consumption in 2022,
renewable energy offers the potential to tackle
issues around energy access, dependency, and
security. (SDG 7)
Air pollution levels are high, particularly in
urban areas, with over 1,600 premature
deaths attributed to air pollution annually.
Waste management and water quality are also
concerning,threatening ecosystems and human
and animal health. While per capita waste
generation has increased, only 0.7 per cent is
recycled compared to 48 per cent in the EU.
(SDGs 13 and 15)
North Macedonia has made some progress in
public administration reform in recent years,
although performance remains among the
weakest in the region. Revenue collection is
undermined by low effective tax rates, sizeable
exemptions, and the informal economy. High
mandatory spending on public wages, underexecuted capital investments, and insufficient
targeted subsidies limit the efficiency of public
spending. Local governments generate only 25
per cent of their revenues, providing further
opportunity to boost fiscal decentralization and
reducing dependence on the central budget.
Corruption remains persistent, with North
Macedonia ranked 88 out of 180 countries
in Transparency International’s Corruption
Perceptions Index 2024. As such, more
effective and accountable governance, fiscal
policies, and budget execution will be critical in
boosting pubic trust and ensuring that growth
and public spending are both sustainable and
inclusive. (SDG 16)
The country’s National Development Strategy
2024–2044, in conjunction with the EU
accession process, provide key opportunities
in addressing the abovementioned challenges
and in progressing towards the SDGs, with
estimates indicating a 24.8 per cent increase in
GDP per capita and a 5.4 per cent reduction in
poverty rates by 2044 should all NDS priorities
be realized.
Leave no one Behind
Discrimination, social exclusion, and
intersectional vulnerabilities continue to impact
a wide range of groups, with women, children,
young people, and minority populations
The country has made remarkable progress
with a tenfold decline in child, infant, and
neonatal mortality rates, already achieving
SDG targets in this area.
10particularly affected, resulting in persistent
inequalities. (SDG 10)
Rooted in persistent stereotypes and unequal
access to economic and political opportunities,
gender inequality remains a major issue. While
women have made significant progress in
parliamentary representation — increasing
from 32 per cent in 2018 to 39.2 per cent in
2025 — they remain underrepresented at
ministerial and mayoral levels. , Women also
made up less than 32 per cent of senior and
middle managementroles in 2025.
Women face higher rates of unemployment
and lower labour force participation, especially
Roma women and those in rural areas. While
women represent 42 per cent of all household
farm workers in individual agricultural holdings,
only 5–12 per cent own land. Fourteen per
cent of women surveyed in 2018 reported
having experienced physical or sexual violence
since the age of 15 at the hands of a partner
or non-partner. Between 2018–2023, women
represented 53 per cent of identified survivors
of human trafficking, of which 40 per cent were
Roma women. Based on the latest publicly
available data (MICS 2019), child marriage
remains a concern with eight per cent of all
women aged 20-24 years having firstmarried or
were in a union before they were 18 years old,
with 45 per cent of Roma women first married
or in union before they were 18 years old, and
15 per cent before age 15. (SDG 5)
A third of children are living in poverty —
substantially higher than the overall poverty
rate — with 40 per cent experiencing multidimensional poverty. , Seventy-three per cent
of children experience violent discipline at
home and approximately 20,000 lack effective
healthcare coverage. Less than 37 per cent
of children aged between 3 and 6 years have
access to pre-primary education, while Roma
children are four times less likely to attend preschool than the national average. , Around 20
per cent of Roma children are consistently out
of school, peaking at nearly 60 per cent in upper
secondary, often driven by socioeconomic
exclusion and resulting in early marriage,
especially amongst girls. Half of all children
with a disability do not transition to secondary
education due to a lack of support measures.
Young people face age-based discrimination,
limited job prospects and vocational training
opportunities, and a lack of voice in decisionmakingwhichcontributetohighratesofoutward
migration. Older adults suffer from ageism,
inadequate pensions, and poor healthcare
access. People with disabilities encounter
widespread ableism, high unemployment,
poor physical accessibility, and exclusion from
public life. Psychosocial disabilities remain
largely unrecognized, limiting access to
support. Physical barriers and lack of accessible
information hinder everyday participation in
various aspects of life.
Refugees,migrants,andstatelesspeoplegrapple
with xenophobia, limited access to education,
employment, healthcare, and legal aid. Ethnic
minorities face persistent discrimination, poor
living conditions, and limited access to essential
services.LGBTQI+individuals facehomophobia,
restricted rights, and vulnerability, while people
living with HIV and sex workers face stigma,
exclusion, and limited access to healthcare and
support services.
Addressing the underlying causes of
vulnerability and exclusion in North Macedonia
will require concerted efforts across all
aspects of governance and society based
on the principle of leaving no one behind. In
addition, empowering those most at-risk and
marginalized — including through inclusive
initiatives and legal protections — will be a
prerequisite for a more cohesive society and for
advancing developmentthatis truly sustainable.
11In preparation for the development of the UN
Cooperation Framework, the UN in North
Macedonia undertook a comprehensive,
integrated, and multidimensional analysis of the
situation in the country through the lens of the
SDGs and the‘Leave no one behind’principle.
The resulting UN Country Analysis identified
key development pathways and catalytic areas
of focus that would have the greatest potential
to accelerate the achievement of multiple SDGs.
The development process was also informed
by the findings and recommendations of an
independent evaluation of the expiring UN
Cooperation Framework 2021–2025.
Extensive consultations were undertaken
with Government counterparts, international
development partners, civil society, and other
stakeholdersonhowtheUNcouldbestcontribute
towards sustainable and inclusive development
in the country, and to prioritize areas of focus
in which the UN potential to make the greatest
impact. More than 70 representatives from
Government, international partners and donors
participated in the prioritization workshops. In
addition, the UN consulted with the UN Youth
Advisory Panel, NGOs working on genderissues
and other members of the civil society.
As the UN Cooperation Framework represents
the UN’s collective offer in support of the
Government of North Macedonia’s national
development priorities, identification of the
below Strategic Priorities was heavily informed
by and aligned to the National Development
Strategy 2024–2044 (see Figure 1).
• Strategic Priority 1: Inclusive Social and
Human Development
• Strategic Priority 2: Sustainable Economy
and Decent Work
• Strategic Priority 3: Resilient and Green
Society and Ecosystems
• Strategic Priority 4: Rule of Law and Good
Governance
These Strategic Priorities also contribute
to the EU’s‘Western Balkans Reform and
Growth Facility 2024–2027’ that articulate
the milestones to advance North Macedonia’s
accession process to the bloc. Additionally,
the Priorities mirror the 5Ps of sustainable
development, namely People, Prosperity, Planet,
and Peace — with Partnerships being inherent
across all priorities — and reflect the‘Six
Transitions’and four‘Engine Room Actions’ to
accelerate progress towards the SDGs.
3.2 Theory of Change for
the Cooperation Framework
Priorities
Advancement towards the SDGs in North
Macedonia will require an integrated, inclusive,
multidimensional, and coordinated approach
across all partners and stakeholders working in
the country towards a common vision and goals.
Developed with the support and engagement
of the UN and based on extensive consultations
engaging over 14,000 citizens, the National
Development Strategy outlines a comprehensive
roadmap and rationale for the accelerated,
inclusive,balanced,gender-equal,andsustainable
development of North Macedonia. The goals,
strategic areas, and priorities of the Strategy
provide the framework and pathways for the
catalyticchangesrequiredforthistooccur.North
Macedonia’s journey towards EU accession
is also considered a key factor in this regard.
To ensure common understanding and logical
coherence in the UN’s support of national
priorities, the theory of change for this UN
Cooperation Framework draws heavily from
that oftheNDS, including itsVision which states:
“People in North Macedonia have a high
quality of life, achieving success in an economy
that is sustainable, competitive and offers
equal opportunities. Institutions are open,
accountable, responsible, innovative, efficient
and open to civil participation. The communities
in which we live are safe, green, resilient to

Increased productivity; 2) Governance models

The UN’s contribution to the NDS will similarly
focus on inclusive social and human development
through strengthening national capacities of
various stakeholders for the delivery of quality,
inclusive, resilient, and sustainable social
services — including health, education, and social
protection — as well as ensuring a coherent
and integrated approach to tackling genderbased violence. Strengthening governance and
institutional capacities to deliver quality services
will further strengthen the social contract
between the state and its population and foster
greater social cohesion. Ensuring equitable
access to quality social services will also enhance
the country’s human capital and equip the next

Advancing sustainable economic development
and the creation of decent work towards a just
transition will require a policy and regulatory
environment, as well as a supportive business
enabling environment that stimulates private
sector-led growth in rural and urban areas
and builds resilience to economic and other
shocks that may impact the country’s economy.
Ensuring that the labour force meet evolving
labour market needs will require a population
that have the necessary knowledge and skills
acquired through capacitated public and private
institutions. Women’s economic empowerment,
including greater participation in the labour
force — including in leadership positions — will
further contribute to equitable growth, help
address labour market shortages, as well as
reduce inequalities, particularly for vulnerable
groups of women.
Tackling that triple planetary crisis will require
a concerted and multidimensional approach to
mitigate and respond to the impacts of climate
change, pollution, and biodiversity loss, as well as
other potential crises. This willrequire improved
gender-responsive legislative and policy
frameworks and enforcement mechanisms, as
well as increased knowledge, capacities, and
resources at national and local levels to ensure a
multipronged approach. In addition to increasing
resilience to climate change and disaster
risks, efforts in this regard will also contribute
towards improving, public health and sustainable
economic development.
Strengthening good governance will be critical
to making progress across all NDS and UN
Cooperation Framework priorities. Ensuring
sustainable and balanced development across
the country will require effective, accountable,
and inclusive institutions at national and local
levels that are capable of meeting the needs
of all people in North Macedonia, particularly
those in vulnerable situations and those
traditionally marginalized, including women,
young people, and civil society. This will require
a policy and regulatory framework that is in
line with international norms and standards, as
well as justice sector and oversight institutions
capable of upholding human rights and the rule
of law. Such initiatives will not only ensure that
governance is responsive to the needs of all
people in the country but will also strengthen the
social contract between the Government and its
people and strengthen social cohesion.
The UN Cooperation Framework is also
underpinned by various cross-cutting
principles that will inform its work across all
outcome areas, including Leave no one behind;
Gender equality and women’s Empowerment;
Human rights-based approach; Sustainability;
Accountability; Resilience; and Participation and
inclusion. In addition, the UN in the Republic
of North Macedonia stands committed to the
full implementation of the Convention on the
Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD) and
the Secretary General’s 2019 UN Disability
Inclusion Strategy and to mobilizing efforts
towards inclusion and non-discrimination of
persons with disabilities in the country.
While the UN Cooperation Framework is
structured against four separate priorities and
outcomes, realization of its development results
will require looking beyond silos and leveraging
synergies and complementarities across the
UN Cooperation Framework’s priorities and
outcomes towards the achievement of higherlevel objectives.The UN system brings extensive
knowledge and expertise that can continue to
contribute towards North Macedonia’s national
development priorities. In addition to in-country
capacities,the UN presence in North Macedonia
can leverage regional and global expertise
and best practices in economic and social
development, climate action and environmental
issues, good governance, human rights, and the
rule of law. In contributing to the achievement of
the development results of the UN Cooperation
Framework, the UN can also apply its collective
mandates and comparative advantages to:

and standards and promotion and protection

perspective;

use;

sustainable way;

of stakeholders working towards sustainable
development in North Macedonia — each with
their own respective mandates and comparative
advantages — the UN will collaborate with a
broad range of partners at national and subnational levels in the implementation of the UN
Cooperation Framework. These include, but
are not limited to, Government partners, nongovernmental organizations, civil society,women
and youth groups, organizations of persons with
disabilities, international development partners,
private sector entities, social partners, and
educational institutions (see Section 3.2 below
on specific partners to be engaged under each
outcome area).

The UN will commission an independent and
impartial external final evaluation of the UN
Cooperation Framework in the penultimate
year of implementation. Coordination with
the Government of North Macedonia on the

accountability, support learning, and inform
decisions regarding the design of the subsequent
UN Cooperation Framework. The evaluation will
systematically assess the contributions of the UN
Cooperation Framework by focusing on achieved
development results in terms of their relevance,
effectiveness, efficiency and sustainability, as well
as the application of cross-cutting themes and
principles, including to Leave No One Behind. The
evaluation will be participatory and seek to assess
the impact of the UN Cooperation Framework on
the lives of people in North Macedonia, especially
vulnerable groups, who will be engaged during the
evaluation process.

evaluation deliverables to ensure that they meet
